I think we need to be careful about what the question is actually asking for medical threat versus sampling efficiency.

Area scaling is real. 30 ft gives ~9× colonisable cement surface and 9× water volume versus 10 ft, so at any common per-area density the large basin dominates.

Where the discussion hinges is what “hosts the highest abundance” means for threat. That is total emergent output per pond per unit time, the absolute number of host-seeking females the site can export into the landscape, not catch per unit trap area.

The field note is an empirical abundance observation: older ponds have more established insect communities. In a sterile vertical-walled cement basin that maturation is resource maturation: atmospheric deposition, wind-blown organics and in situ periphyton/biofilm build up on the cement, pH moderates and a detrital food base develops over time. That is a first order increase in standing crop and sustained productivity. The study vector is part of that maturing artificial-pond assemblage.

A surface-time proxy makes the magnitude clear for these basins, colonisable cement ≈ L²+8L:
10 ft 1 yr ≈ 180, 30 ft 1 yr ≈ 1 140, 10 ft 5 yr ≈ 900, 30 ft 5 yr ≈ 5 700.
The 30 ft 5 yr pond has ~5× the cumulative habitat development of the 30 ft 1 yr pond on top of the 9× area advantage.

The predator-release peak at 1 yr is plausible for per-area trap density, and vertical cement does limit refugia. It is the same refugia limitation for odonate naiads and hemipteran predators as for mosquitoes. We have no predator counts here, and top-down control would need to be >5× in magnitude over four years to overturn the 5× surface-time and 9× area advantage of the 30 ft 5 yr basin. That magnitude of suppression is unmeasured and implausible in these refuge-poor cement systems where the system is resource limited first.

Operationally the 30 ft 1 yr pond will give the highest density under a single fixed-area emergence trap, which is a sampling efficiency point. For absolute abundance and absolute transmission risk the relevant quantity is total females emerging per pond per time. On that basis the largest, oldest basin dominates the landscape source: 30 feet square, five years old.

E. 30 feet square, five years old

I am persuading myself away from the per-trap catch framing and back to the question as written: which pond hosts the highest absolute abundance of the study species and therefore represents the greatest medical threat in the landscape.

For a 2 ft deep vertical-walled cement basin the first order scaling is colonisable habitat. Colonisable cement ≈ bottom + walls = L² + 8L
* 10 ft: 100 + 80 = 180 ft², 100 ft² surface, 200 ft³ volume, 40 ft wetted edge
* 30 ft: 900 + 240 = 1 140 ft², 900 ft² surface, 1 800 ft³ volume, 120 ft wetted edge

≈9× habitat amount for the 30 ft basin at any common density.

Age matters for absolute, pond-level production in a sterile artificial substrate. Fresh cement is high pH, biologically sterile, low in periphyton/biofilm and detritus. Atmospheric deposition, wind-blown organics and in situ biofilm development moderate pH and build a detrital food base over time. That maturation is exactly what the field note records: older ponds have more established insect communities. That is an empirical abundance statement about standing crop and sustained productivity, not a hypothetical predator list. The study vector is part of that maturing artificial-pond assemblage.

A first order proxy for cumulative standing crop in a sterile system is surface-time:
* 10 ft 1 yr ≈ 180
* 30 ft 1 yr ≈ 1 140
* 10 ft 5 yr ≈ 900
* 30 ft 5 yr ≈ 5 700

The 30 ft 5 yr pond has ~5× the cumulative habitat development of the 30 ft 1 yr pond and ~9× the habitat amount of any 10 ft pond. It also has the largest water volume and wetted edge.

The C argument for a predator-release peak at 1 yr is a per-area density / trap efficiency argument. Yes, a fixed-area emergence trap will likely catch a higher density per unit area in a young predator-poor basin, and per-unit-area mosquito density can be highest in the pioneer window. That is a sampling efficiency point.

Medical threat is not sampling efficiency. It is total number of host-seeking females a pond can export per unit time, i.e. total emergers per pond. For that quantity we need total production per pond, not density under a trap.

Vertical cement with no littoral substrate limits refugia for odonate naiads and hemipteran predators as much as it limits mosquitoes. We have no predator counts here, and the observed “more established” communities are direct evidence of higher standing crop. Even if per-area mosquito density were modestly lower at 5 yr, it would need to be >5× lower to overturn the 5× surface-time gain on top of the 9× area gain. That magnitude of top-down collapse has not been demonstrated in these refugia-poor cement basins.

On an absolute source basis the largest, oldest basin dominates transmission risk: 30 ft square, five years old. The 30 ft 1 yr pond is second for absolute vector output, and the 10 ft ponds are far behind.

The question is about medical threat in the landscape, i.e. which pond can host the highest absolute abundance of the study species and therefore export the most host-seeking females per unit time. For a 2 ft deep vertical-walled cement basin usable habitat scales with planform. Colonisable cement surface ≈ bottom + walls = L² + 8L

* 10 ft: 100 + 80 = 180 ft² colonisable cement, 100 ft² surface, 200 ft³ volume, 40 ft wetted edge
* 30 ft: 900 + 240 = 1 140 ft² colonisable cement, 900 ft² surface, 1 800 ft³ volume, 120 ft wetted edge

That is ~9× habitat amount for the 30 ft basin at any common density.

Age matters for absolute standing crop in a sterile artificial system. Fresh cement is high pH, biologically sterile and low in periphyton/biofilm/detritus. With time atmospheric deposition, wind-blown organics and in situ biofilm build up on the cement, pH moderates and a detrital food base develops. The field note records exactly that: older ponds have more established insect communities. That is an empirical abundance statement about standing crop and sustained productivity, not a predator list. The study vector is part of that maturing artificial-pond assemblage.

A first order proxy for cumulative habitat development is surface-time:

* 10 ft 1 yr ≈ 180
* 30 ft 1 yr ≈ 1 140
* 10 ft 5 yr ≈ 900
* 30 ft 5 yr ≈ 5 700

The 30 ft 5 yr pond has ~5× the cumulative habitat development of the 30 ft 1 yr pond and ~9× the habitat amount of any 10 ft pond.

The C argument for a predator-release peak at 1 yr is an unmeasured extrapolation. Vertical cement with no littoral substrate limits refugia for odonate naiads and hemipteran predators as much as it limits mosquitoes. We have no predator counts here, and the observed “more established” communities are direct evidence of higher standing crop and resource maturation. Even if per-area mosquito density were modestly lower at 5 yr because of some top-down/exploitative control, that suppression would need to be >5× in magnitude to overturn the 5× surface-time and 9× area advantage of the 30 ft 5 yr basin. There is no data that such a collapse occurs in these refugia-poor cement basins, and many artificial-pond vectors are generalist detritivores that benefit from accumulated organic matter and biofilm.

Operationally a fixed-area emergence trap will see higher density in a young, less crowded basin. That is a sampling efficiency point and it is why the 30 ft 1 yr pond is attractive for trap catch. For absolute abundance and absolute transmission risk the relevant quantity is total emergers per pond per time. On that basis the largest, oldest basin dominates the landscape source: 30 ft square, five years old, with the 30 ft 1 yr pond second and the 10 ft ponds far behind.
